segments.say: Phase one. One agent, reading the plan we wrote in the last lecture, turning six areas of prose into a list of jobs a program can execute. Look at what is actually in this repository before it starts. Node modules, a tools folder with one script in it, a gitignore, BRIEF dot md, CLAUDE dot md, two package files and plan dot md. Not one line of product code. Signal Desk at this moment is entirely prose. And almost every one of those files carries a U beside it, with main and a star in the status bar, which means nothing in here has been committed yet - the whole repository is untracked. Fix that before a run like this. A commit costs five seconds and turns the next twenty minutes from a mystery into a diff. And this is the step that people skip, so it is worth saying what it is for. The plan is written for a person. It has reasoning in it, and cross-references, and a paragraph about what to do if a contract turns out to be wrong. None of that is executable. What the runner needs is much smaller and much stricter: for each job, an identifier, the files it owns, the tools it is allowed, the jobs it has to wait for, and a brief written for somebody who cannot ask a question. Turning the first into the second is a translation, and it is the kind of translation a model is genuinely good at - it is reading comprehension with a schema on the end of it. And look at the command that started it. Orchestrator dot mjs, then the word plan. Not run. This runner has two verbs, and the fact that they are two rather than one is the most useful decision in the file. Between them, tasks dot json exists on disk and nothing has been built. That gap is your review gate. You can open the file, delete a job, tighten a brief, change a dependency, and only then type run. A single command that plans and builds in one breath takes that away, and it takes it away at the exact moment when a bad decision is cheapest to fix. Four minutes. Three hundred and sixty-six lines. That is the whole orchestrator - the planner, the worker pool, the reviewer, the log, the table at the end. Sit with that number, because the instinct when you hear the words agent orchestration is that there must be a framework under it. There is a loop, a set of promises, and one function that decides which jobs are eligible. And the line above it is the entire dependency footprint: at anthropic dash a i slash claude dash agent dash s d k, already up to date, a hundred and four packages audited, no vulnerabilities. Right now that line ending in three dots is everything you get. One agent is reading plan dot md, it will print again when it has finished, and in between there is no token stream and no partial output - just a cursor. That is a property of calling the SDK this way rather than a limitation. It returns a result, not a conversation. It also means the one thing you would want here, a line the moment it starts on each section, is something you have to write yourself. And notice the one thing this phase is not allowed to do: build anything. It has read, glob, grep and write, and the only file it writes is the task list. That separation matters more than it looks. A planner that can also build will, given a hard task, quietly do the task instead of planning it - and you will end up with one agent having written a third of the product before the other six have started, in files they were about to be given ownership of. There is a second reason to make the planner its own agent, and it is about blast radius. This one is pointed at a repository with no source in it, and the worst thing it can produce is a bad tasks dot json, which you can read in thirty seconds. The build phase gets bash, and edits, and a working tree to damage. Keeping the cheap reviewable step apart from the expensive destructive one is not an orchestration idea. It is the same instinct as running the risky command inside the sandbox. And notice that its input is a file in the repository rather than something typed at a prompt. Plan dot md is sitting there in the rail, versioned alongside the code it is about to cause. When a build comes out wrong, and your first one will, the question you have to answer is whether the plan was wrong or the execution was - and you can only answer it if the plan is still on disk exactly as the planner read it. One more thing about those four minutes. They are the cheapest four minutes in this lecture, and they decide almost everything that follows. There is a shape to that translation worth naming, because you will do it by hand at least once. A plan is written to be understood; a task list is written to be executed. The difference is not detail - the plan has more detail. It is that every sentence in a task list has to survive being read by somebody with no context, no colleagues and no way to ask, and most sentences in most plans do not.

And here is what it decided the work is. Seven jobs. Tasks dot json has appeared in the rail, and that file is the artefact here, not the sentence in the terminal. Everything from now on reads it. Seven, from six areas - the extra one is a cross-cutting verification job it added at the end that the plan does not name. Read that as a small warning as well as a nice touch: a planner given latitude will use it, and the thing it adds is the thing you did not review.

Read the dependency column, because that is the whole plan compressed into one line each. The simulator waits for nothing. The rules engine waits for the simulator. The server waits for both. The two client halves wait for nothing at all, because they were given contracts rather than code. The app shell waits for the server and both clients. And a verification pass at the end waits for everything. That is a shape you could draw on a napkin, and it came out of a document nobody wrote as a graph. Now phase two, and this is the one to watch. Two redirections in that command, and both matter: standard error folded into standard output, and the whole stream teed into build dot out. If a job throws, the trace lands in the same file as the timeline, in order, rather than in a scrollback. And read what a brief looks like in there, because it is not the sentence I would have typed. Each one names the files that job owns, restates the contract it has to honour, and says what it must not touch - all copied forward out of the plan. Nobody is going to be available to clarify any of it. That is the actual design constraint on an unattended run, and it is why the planning phase is a separate agent rather than a paragraph in the runner. And the graph it chose is not the only correct one. The server waits for the finished rules engine, and it did not have to - the rules engine's interface is written out in the plan exactly as the simulator's is, so the server could have been built against the contract and started at minute zero with the others. That single edge is most of this build's critical path, and it was a judgement call made by a planning agent in four minutes that nobody reviewed.

Three start at once: the simulator, the watchlist and chart, and the rules and alerts panels. And watch the left rail, because for the next quarter of an hour it is the only thing on this screen that moves. Simulator, test and public are already sitting there, three directories that did not exist ninety seconds ago. The terminal will not print another word until the whole run finishes, so a folder appearing is your only live signal that anything is happening at all. And I want to be precise about why those two client jobs can start before anything they depend on exists, because it is the single most useful idea in this lecture. They are not building against the simulator. They are building against the description of what the simulator returns, which was written down in the plan an hour ago. The code they consume does not exist yet and it does not need to. That is what a contract is for, and it is why the hour we spent on the plan buys three jobs of parallelism here. There is something quietly good in that rail worth pointing at. Test arrived in the same breath as simulator. Nobody asked for that in the run command; it is in the brief, because it was in the plan, because we wrote it there an hour ago. That is what a brief written for somebody who cannot ask a question buys you - the standards travel with the job instead of living in your head. And be clear about what a new folder proves, which is nothing. It is evidence of a write. All the rail tells you is that an agent is alive. There is a second thing worth seeing in that first minute, which is what does not start. The rules engine is eligible on paper - the limit is three and only three are running - but it declared the simulator as a dependency, so the scheduler is holding it. That is not politeness. Building a rules engine against a simulator that does not exist yet means inventing the shape of a candle, and inventing it slightly differently from whoever eventually writes it. And there is a version of this you should not do, which I have watched people do. Given seven jobs and a concurrency limit, the instinct is to set the limit to seven. Three is not a compromise. Each of these is reading the same plan and the same memory file and writing into the same working tree, and past three the contention stops being about compute and starts being about the repository - two agents installing something, two agents editing the same package file, two agents both deciding to create a directory. There is one more thing worth saying about starting three, and it is about you rather than the machine. Three is small enough that you can hold what they are doing in your head. Seven is not. The moment you cannot say out loud what each running agent is currently working on, you have stopped supervising and started hoping - and the concurrency limit is the only dial that decides which of those you are doing.

And now the thing that is genuinely strange about watching this, which is that there is nothing to watch. No dashboard. No panes to cycle through. No approval prompts. Two of the files at the bottom of the rail have gone grey. Build dot out and run dot log are both matched by the gitignore, which is the sensible default and also the thing to reconsider here. The only record of how this build happened is the one artefact that will not survive a clone. Three agents are writing into this repository at the same time and the entire interface to that is a log file and a shell that has not returned yet. Compare that with Thursday, where the whole screen was a team talking to each other and you could go and read any one of them. Both of those are real ways to run this work, and the difference is not quality. It is whether you intend to be in the room. And there is a real cost to not being in the room, which I want to name rather than skip. On Thursday, when a teammate found a gap between two other teammates' ownership, it reported it and the lead absorbed the work. Nothing here can do that. If one of these seven hits something that belongs to nobody, it will either do it anyway - in files it does not own - or leave it. There is no channel. That is the price of the interface being a log file. What you can do with this time, and what I would actually do on a real project, is write down what you are going to check when it comes back. Before you see the result, because the result is persuasive. Does every area in the plan have files on disk. Does the suite pass. Does the thing start. Is there anything in the brief that no file addresses. Four questions, written down while you have nothing else to do, and they are worth more than any amount of watching the log. And there is something worth saying about how this feels, because it is not how a build normally feels and the difference matters. Nothing is asking you for anything. There is no point at which your attention is required, and therefore no point at which it is invited. Every other tool in this course has been a conversation, and a conversation has turns. This has none. If you sit here you are not supervising, you are just present - and the honest thing to do with the next quarter of an hour is something else entirely. And there is a version of this that would have been faster, which is worth saying while nothing is happening. If the server had been given the rules engine's contract instead of the finished rules engine, it could have started at minute zero with the two client jobs. That one edge in the graph is most of this build's duration. It was a judgement made in four minutes by a planning agent, and reviewing that judgement is about ninety seconds of work that nobody did, including me.

The simulator lands first, at about a minute and a half, and the moment it does the rules engine starts - because the scheduler was holding it, and it stops holding it the instant its dependency reports done. Nobody is coordinating that. It is thirty lines of JavaScript we read five minutes ago. You can see the shape of that in the rail. Rules is there now, sitting between public and simulator, and it was not there when the run started. The areas in the plan are arriving as top-level directories, one at a time, in dependency order. That is the closest thing to a progress bar this build has, and we got it by accident - because we happened to tell every job which files it owns. And look at what the log line actually records: a timestamp, the job, the event, the area, and how long it took. Five fields. That is enough to reconstruct this entire run afterwards, and it is roughly one line of code per field. The reason to write it at the start rather than when you need it is that the run you will most want to understand is the one that went wrong, and that is exactly the run where you will not be watching. And it is worth naming what a dependency actually bought here, because it is not ordering for its own sake. The rules engine consumes candles. If it had started at the same moment as the simulator, it would have had to decide for itself what a candle looks like - and the plan does document that, so it might well have got it right. But might have is the whole problem. The dependency turns a document that could be misread into a file that can be read. So what would going wrong look like from here? Not an error. The rail would simply stop changing and the shell would not come back, and there is no visible difference between an agent thinking hard and an agent that has wedged. The only thing that separates them is the clock. Open run dot log, find the last start line, and compare its timestamp with now. If a job you expected to take three minutes has been open for fifteen, that is your answer, and you got it from a file rather than from staring at a cursor. The rule worth taking home is smaller than it sounds. Give every job one artefact it must produce, and name that artefact in the brief. Then the file system is a status board you did not have to build. It is worth being clear about what a dependency is not, as well. It is not a statement that one job is more important than another, and it is not politeness about who goes first. It is a claim that one job cannot be done correctly until another has finished. Every dependency you add that is not that is a parallel job you have thrown away, and on a plan of this size that is minutes.

And this is a good moment to talk about what this is costing, because a lecture that shows you seven agents and not the bill is selling something. Each of these is a full session with its own context, reading the plan, reading the memory file, reading whatever else it needs, and then writing several files. Seven of those is not seven times one question. And there is a piece of arithmetic on this screen that undercuts the whole idea of a pool. Server is in the rail now, which means the server job is running. The two client jobs finished minutes ago. The rules engine is done. So right now, with a concurrency limit of three, exactly one agent is working, and the other two slots are empty and will stay empty for the rest of the build. If you are going to run something like this, run it on a repository you can afford to run it on twice, because the first version of your task list will be wrong. The other half of the cost question is the one you cannot see on this screen at all, which is what each of these is reading. Every one of them opens the plan and the memory file before it does anything else, because that is how it learns what it owns. Seven agents, seven copies of the same two documents. Which is the arithmetic argument for keeping the memory file short that we made on Wednesday, and here it is being paid, seven times over, in one eighteen-minute window. Which makes the honest answer to what this costs: less than you would fear, and for the wrong reason. Seven agents is the headline. One at a time is the reality, for most of this run. If you are budgeting a build like this, the number to estimate is not how many jobs there are - it is how many of them can genuinely overlap, and on this plan that turned out to be three, for four minutes, right at the beginning. It changes what you should measure, too. Not agents launched, and not jobs completed. Agent-minutes sitting on the critical path, because that is the only number a better plan can move. There is also a thing worth saying about failure here, since none of these have failed. If one of them does, the runner marks it failed and skips everything downstream, and you get a table at the end with a gap in it. That is much better than the alternative, which is a build where the server was written against a simulator that does not exist and everything looks finished. A partial build you can see is worth more than a complete one you cannot trust. And the other reason to keep a log rather than rely on the terminal is that the terminal is not yours. It scrolls, it gets cleared, it belongs to whichever window happens to be open. A file in the repository outlives all of that, and it is the only artefact from this run that will still exist when somebody asks in November why the server was written before the front end.

The server started when both the simulator and the rules engine were done, and the app shell cannot start until the server does. So for a stretch in the middle here, the concurrency limit of three is not the constraint at all - the shape of the plan is. And look at what the rail is doing now, which is nothing. Server was the last directory to appear, a few minutes back. Whatever the app shell is writing is going into folders that already exist, so for this entire stretch the file tree is flat. The one live signal we had has gone quiet, and it has gone quiet during the longest job in the run. There is a chain down the middle of this build, and while it is running, most of the capacity is idle. Which exposes a real defect in our three hundred and sixty-six lines, and it is worth naming rather than editing out. This runner appends a line when a job starts and a line when it finishes, and nothing in between. On a job that takes six minutes, that is six minutes in which a healthy run and a hung one look identical from here. The fix is small - one line appended every thirty seconds with the job id and its elapsed time, a heartbeat rather than a spinner - and the reason to write it before you need it is that the run you will want it for is the one you are not sitting in front of. There is also a better answer than staring, and you already have it. Every one of these agents is writing to disk as it works. If you need to know whether that job is alive, you do not read the log at all - you check modification times in the working tree from a second terminal. A build that is progressing touches files, every few seconds. That check takes two seconds, and it does not depend on anyone having remembered to print anything. And notice what the log gives you that the terminal does not. The terminal shows you now. The log shows you the order things happened in, afterwards, when you are trying to work out why an area looks wrong. Every one of these lines costs one append and they are the only reason the next lecture can say anything precise about this run at all. There is a smaller thing in the log worth noticing while it goes past. Each line names the area, in the plan's own words, not just the task id. That is the sort of detail that costs nothing to write and saves ten minutes at the moment you are trying to work out which of six directories a failure belongs to. It is also, quietly, the thing that makes a build like this reviewable at all. Nobody is going to read two thousand three hundred lines of generated code line by line. What you can read is fourteen log lines and seven diffs, and decide from those which two of the seven are worth reading properly.

Which is worth knowing before you go and build one of these, because the obvious instinct when a build is slow is to raise the concurrency limit, and here that would do nothing whatsoever. Start with the number you can work out from the task list still sitting in the terminal. Seven jobs, three slots. If they were all independent, three at a time would clear seven jobs in three rounds. Instead the graph runs simulator, then rules engine, then server, then app shell, then the verification pass - a chain of five, with two client jobs hanging off the side. Five of the seven are in a queue, and no scheduler makes a queue shorter. The thing that would make this faster is a different plan - one where the server does not need the finished rules engine, only its contract, exactly as the two client jobs did. That decision was made an hour ago in a document, and it is being paid for now. There is a general version of that worth carrying out of this lecture. The speed-up from running agents in parallel is bounded by the longest chain of things that genuinely have to happen in order, and that chain is decided when you write the plan, not when you run it. Every contract you write down properly turns a dependency into a parallel job. Every one you leave vague turns a parallel job into a queue. There is a tell for which edges are which, and it is a one-sentence test. A dependency you can justify by saying this job consumes what that job produces is real. A dependency you justify by saying it makes more sense to do that one first is not a dependency, it is a preference, and you are paying minutes for it. Ours has one of each. The one that cost us was written by an agent in four minutes and reviewed by nobody, including me. It is worth doing that arithmetic on your own plan before you run it, and it takes about a minute. Write down each area, what it waits for, and roughly how long you think it takes. Add up the longest path. That number is your build time, and no scheduler is going to beat it. And do that arithmetic on the plan, not on the task list, because by the time a planning agent has turned your prose into a graph the interesting decision has already been taken. The place to fix a chain is the paragraph describing the second job, where you either wrote down what the first one hands over or you did not. Two sentences of interface, written before anybody builds anything, buy more than any amount of tuning the runner ever will. And it changes what a slow build means. On a normal project, slow means the machine is busy and you buy a faster one. Here the machine is idle and the plan is serial, and the fix is a document, not hardware. That is a genuinely new failure mode and it is worth having a name for.

The app shell is the longest single job in the run, and that makes sense: it is the piece that has to reconcile everybody else's decisions. Five separate agents each wrote something that exposes an interface, and this one has to wire all of them into one page, in the browser, with the container ids they each assumed. It runs for about six and a half minutes, longer than the simulator and the server put together, and integration is where the time goes on every build shaped like this one. The reason is not that a shell is complicated. It is that five other agents each made a small decision alone, in isolation, with no way to check it against anybody, and the last one has to make all five of those decisions agree without being allowed to change any of them. Nobody plans for that to be the expensive part. It always is. And this is the moment where the whole thing is most likely to go wrong, which is worth saying out loud even though it did not. Everyone else has finished and gone. If the shell finds that two of them disagree about a container id, or about the shape of what the feed sends, there is nobody left to ask. It either resolves the disagreement by reading their code, or it guesses. And a guess here is the worst kind of defect, because it does not fail. It compiles. The page loads, one panel is empty, and there is nothing in any log to tell you why, because from the shell's point of view nothing went wrong. That is the specific failure of unattended work to scan for afterwards - not crashes, which announce themselves, but silent disagreements that got resolved in favour of whoever wrote last. You will not find those by running the build again either. A second run makes different guesses. That is the failure mode of an unattended build, and the reason the review phase exists. And this is where an unattended build differs most sharply from the team on Thursday. There, the lead was still in the conversation and could ask. Here, everyone who could answer has already exited. Whatever the shell agent finds, it resolves alone, from the code in front of it. So what do you do about that, given that you were not here? You read the seams first. Not the six diffs in order - the handful of places where two areas had to agree on a name, a shape or an event, and you check those before you look at anything else. That is a quarter of an hour of reading, and it finds the one class of defect this run was most likely to produce. The rest of a generated diff is either obviously fine or obviously broken. The seams are the only part that is quietly wrong. There is a decision worth making before you ever run one of these, and this is the beat that makes the case for it: give one job the remit to look at the whole thing. Ours has one - the cross-cutting verification pass at the end - and it exists because the planner added it, not because I asked. Write that job into the plan yourself rather than hoping for it. It owns no files, it waits for everything, and its brief is one line per seam: two areas, the thing they had to agree on, and a question. Without it, six agents each finish their own area correctly and nobody ever looks at the seams between them until a person does.

And there is the table. Seven jobs, all done, none failed, none skipped. Seventeen minutes and fifty-three seconds of wall clock, with nobody in the room. But add up the seven job times and you get just under twenty-four - and the difference is not what you would think. Simulator, rules engine, server, shell, verification: that chain is seventeen minutes and fifty-two seconds on its own. Running three at a time did not shorten this build at all. And there is where that comes from. Fourteen lines in run dot log, every start and every finish with a timestamp and a millisecond count. The whole run, reconstructable, out of about one line of code. It just let the two client jobs finish early and wait.
